title: Agent with tools and limits
subtitle: The model proposes, the code executes and a person approves what’s expensive
mission: Aurora’s support wants an agent that handles refund requests: look up the order, work out the amount and return the money. Give it only the tools it needs, a step limit and a human approval rule, and find out what happens when you take the brake off.

predict.question: order 8812 asks for a R$ 1.125,00 refund and Aurora’s policy requires human approval above R$ 500. With the refund tool enabled, the agent…

feedback.right: right: having the tool is not a blank check. The portal’s code checks the amount against the limit, sees it exceeds R$ 500 and stops to ask for approval; nothing is refunded until someone says yes.

why.simples:
An agent is a model that can use tools over several steps: look up, calculate, act. Giving it a tool is like handing the company card to an intern: it works, as long as there’s a spending limit and someone approves the big purchases.
There are three limits: which tools exist, how many steps it may take and from what amount a person must say yes.
why.dev:
The cycle is always the same: the model asks for a tool (in the APIs the response comes with stop_reason "tool_use" and tool-use blocks), your code runs it and returns the result in a tool_result, and the model continues until it answers. The model writes the request; your code executes it, and that’s where the limits live: allowed-tool list, step maximum, argument validation and human approval.
Separate read tools (cheap, no side effects) from write tools (refund, send email, delete). Writes involving money or data go through confirmation, and every call goes to an audit log. The API’s tool_choice parameter lets you force or forbid tools when the flow needs it.
why.especialista:
Think minimal permissions: the agent acts on someone’s behalf and should have, at most, that person’s permission, never a broad credential. Tool results are untrusted input (an order can carry text with instructions), so the limit must live in code, not in the prompt. Use idempotency (a unique key per refund) so retries don’t duplicate money, and step and cost budgets per task so a loop can’t spend forever.
Measure the agent as a system: tasks completed, steps per task, tool errors and denied approvals. Human approval only works if the request is clear (what, how much, why); otherwise it turns into an automatic "ok".

data.sysTools: You are Aurora’s refund assistant. Tools: lookup(key) returns the order data by number; calculator(expression) solves sums with + - * /. The policy only refunds up to 30 days after delivery. ALWAYS reply with a single JSON and nothing else: {"tool":"lookup","args":{"key":"8812"}} or {"tool":"calculator","args":{"expression":"1250*0.9"}} or, when done, {"answer":"REFUND 8812 1125"} (order number and amount) or {"answer":"DENY 7700 outside the window"}. The portal runs the refund, not you.

steps: Pick a flow of yours with an action that changes data (refund, cancellation) and list the tools in two columns: read and write.
Write the agent loop with your provider’s SDK: call the model, run only the tools on the list, return the tool_result and stop at a maximum number of steps.
Put the rule in code: above a value, the write action doesn’t run and produces an approval request with what, how much and why.
recipe.ok: with a small request the agent finishes on its own; with a big one it stops at the approval request, and no write action happens without going through the rule.
